topics.context:
• Yes means they will do it. No means they won't do it.
  • The skill is to have them choose between doing what you want one way or another way. If you want an appointment with Mr. Smith, for example, you might say:

    "Would this afternoon be satisfactory, Mr. Smith, or do you prefer tomorrow morning or afternoon?" (You are giving Mr. Smith a choice of times to see you - a choice of yeses.)

  • The least effective way would be to ask for an appointment. This way you are giving him a choice between yes (you can have the appointment) and no (you can't have the appointment.)

Examples –

"Do you want the black or do you want the white?"
(Rather than, "Do you want one of these?")

"So do you want to start work tomorrow or Tuesday?"
(Rather than, "Do you want to start work?")

"Do you want this charged or do you want to pay cash?"
(Rather than, "Do you want this?")

This method won't work every time, but it will work a good deal of the time. And it will work far better than giving people a choice between saying yes and no.

sentiment.summary: Tips on phrasing choices to elicit affirmative responses.

faqs.question: What does the text mean by "Yes means they will do it. No means they won't do it."
faqs.answer: It explains that when you give someone a choice, a 'yes' indicates they agree to do something, while a 'no' indicates they refuse.

faqs.question: How can I use a choice to get a positive response?
faqs.answer: Offer the person a selection between two options that both lead to the desired outcome, such as asking for a specific time for an appointment instead of simply asking if they can meet.

faqs.question: Why is asking for an appointment considered the least effective way?
faqs.answer: Because it forces the person to choose between a 'yes' (you can meet) and a 'no' (you can't meet), which may lead to a refusal.

faqs.question: Can you give an example of a better way to ask for a choice?
faqs.answer: Yes, for example: "Would this afternoon be satisfactory, Mr. Smith, or do you prefer tomorrow morning or afternoon?" This gives Mr. Smith a choice of times, both of which are acceptable.

faqs.question: What is the purpose of giving people a choice between two options?
faqs.answer: It increases the likelihood that they will say 'yes' because they feel they have control over the decision.

faqs.question: Are there situations where this method might not work?
faqs.answer: The text acknowledges that it won't work every time, but it generally works better than forcing a simple yes/no decision.

faqs.question: What does the text suggest about expecting people to say 'yes'?
faqs.answer: It says that when you expect people to say yes, you are showing confidence, and you should let them know that they are expected to say yes.

faqs.question: How should I phrase a question to give a choice?
faqs.answer: Use a structure that presents two distinct options, such as "Do you want the black or do you want the white?" instead of a single open-ended question.

faqs.question: What is the benefit of giving a choice over a simple yes/no?
faqs.answer: It reduces the chance of a refusal and makes the person feel more involved in the decision, increasing the likelihood of a positive response.

faqs.question: Can you provide another example of a choice-based question?
faqs.answer: Sure: "So do you want to start work tomorrow or Tuesday?" This offers two specific start dates rather than asking if they want to start work at all.

summary.title: Using Choice to Secure Agreement
summary.long_summary: The passage explains a communication technique that increases the likelihood of receiving a positive response by framing options as a choice of "yeses" rather than a simple yes/no question. It begins by defining the difference: a yes means the person will comply, a no means they will not. The core skill is to present the listener with multiple acceptable options, thereby giving them a sense of control and making it easier for them to say yes. For example, instead of asking for an appointment and presenting a binary choice, the speaker offers specific times: "Would this afternoon be satisfactory, Mr. Smith, or do you prefer tomorrow morning or afternoon?" This approach gives Mr. Smith a choice of times, each of which is a yes. The text contrasts this with the less effective method of simply asking for an appointment, which forces the listener into a yes/no decision. It then provides several illustrative examples: asking whether someone wants black or white instead of asking if they want one of these; asking whether to start work tomorrow or Tuesday instead of asking if they want to start work; and asking whether to charge or pay cash instead of asking if they want the item. These examples show how offering distinct, mutually exclusive options can lead to a more favorable outcome. The passage acknowledges that this method does not work in every situation but generally performs better than a simple yes/no question. Finally, it touches on the concept of expecting people to say yes and communicating that expectation, which is described as a form of confidence that goes beyond merely hoping for agreement. The overall message is that by structuring requests as a set of acceptable choices, communicators can increase the likelihood of a positive response and create a more collaborative interaction.
summary.short_summary: Offer choices to elicit affirmative responses.
